summary: Redwood and Synapse Health ran a technical deep dive on multi-region routing, capacity planning and DR playbooks. Key topics: policy routing by latency/cost, regional capacity and burst behavior, KV-cache considerations during failover, batching/throughput tradeoffs, quantization fallbacks, and on-prem/VPC constraints. transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-25 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 mins
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Ravi Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jasmine Cole (Redwood Solutions Eng); Karen Li (CTO, Synapse Health), Marcus Reed (Staff ML Engineer), Olga Petrova (SRE), Henry Wong (Product)

[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna dive into multi-region routing and failover, very much a technical session - Ravi and Jasmine will cover the runtime and DR parts.
[00:18] Karen Li: Thanks, Ava. Quick context - Synapse is live in prod in us-east and eu-west, we're evaluating adding ap-south-east for customer latency. Our main concerns are graceful failover, cache warm-up, and preserving model versioning during cross-region traffic.
[00:35] Ravi Kapoor: Got it. Our agenda is: policy routing rules, capacity signals, KV cache behavior, batching impacts during failover, quantization fallbacks, and VPC/ on-prem considerations. We'll run through example playbooks.
[00:52] Marcus Reed: One quick ask up front: we run heavy L2 summarization workloads with ~90% short sequences and occasional long context. Peak TPS is ~700 reqs/s, p95 latency target 250ms.
[01:10] Jasmine Cole: good, that helps. Ok first - policy routing. The simple model is rules evaluated at the load balancer / control plane: prefer regional low-latency targets (latency <= threshold), then cost tier, then capacity headroom. Policies can be combined; e.g. prefer us-east for customers in NA unless regional p95 crosses threshold or capacity drops below X.
[01:35] Olga Petrova: How do you detect 'capacity drops'? Do you use scheduling signals or direct GPU telemetry?
[01:45] Ravi Kapoor: We ingest both. Node-level telemetry (GPU util, queue depth, token-per-second) and per-model soft limits. The router calculates an active headroom metric; when headroom below 15% we start draining and route new sessions to fallback regions. There's also an emergency mode if control plane can't reach a region.
[02:05] Karen Li: And what about affinity - we need KV cache warm keys for session continuity. If we route to a new region, won't cold cache spike latency?
[02:15] Jasmine Cole: Yes. We recommend sticky routing for warm sessions: maintain session affinity for X minutes (configurable), and when you must fail over, do a gradual split traffic with a prefix-cache repopulation strategy. Two options we discussed: 1) proactive cross-region KV replication for critical customers (tradeoff: bandwidth and consistency), or 2) fast cold-warm ramp: route 10% of session traffic to new region to populate caches, then increase if metrics look ok.
[02:44] Marcus Reed: That 10% idea - how do you ensure safety for correctness? We have hallucination sensitivity and changing model versions.
[02:52] Ravi Kapoor: Good point. We tie rollout/version matching into the router: model version compatibility must be signaled. If the destination doesn't have an exact model version, router can either 1) block routing, 2) route to a compatible quantized variant, or 3) route with a tagged fallback and later reconcile. For high-risk customers you can set failover policy to "same-model-only".
[03:18] Henry Wong: Can you expand on 'quantized variant' as fallback? We worry about quality regression.
[03:25] Jasmine Cole: Sure. Quantized fallback is a way to preserve availability when the full-precision model isn't available in the target region. We keep tuned quantization profiles and a short eval harness to compare outputs on a small canary prompt set. The router attaches a metadata header so the app can detect degraded model and do compensations. We also emit quality regression alerts.
[03:48] Karen Li: Where are those canary evals run - control plane or customer side?
[03:54] Ravi Kapoor: Typically control plane in Redwood - lightweight, customer-provided prompt set. For extra security customers can run evals in their private deployment.
[04:05] Ava Martinez: Quick interjection - we've found that maintaining a small, region-local persistent cache for top-k prefixes reduces cold-start latency dramatically for sessions that matter. It's not feasible for everything, but for high-value tenants it's helpful.
[04:22] Olga Petrova: Regarding networking: if we fail over from us-east to eu-west, our VPC peering and KMS location - keys are in GCP us-east1. How do we manage encryption and compliance?
[04:34] Jasmine Cole: Two options: 1) Customer-managed keys in multiple regions (we can integrate with cross-region KMS replication if provider supports it), or 2) route traffic but proxy encryption so payloads remain in-customer-region-only - but that can add latency. We also support bringing Redwood Private into ap-south-east to avoid cross-border data concerns.
[05:00] Marcus Reed: Ok. About routing triggers - is it purely telemetry thresholds or do you allow manual DR playbook triggers?
[05:07] Ravi Kapoor: Both. We have automated triggers (latency, error spike, capacity) and manual playbooks. Playbooks can be executed via Console API: start incremental failover, enforce immediate global redirect, or run test-mode (shadow traffic). They log steps and are auditable for compliance.
[05:24] Karen Li: Let's talk throughput and batching when traffic moves regions. We saw throughput drop when batch sizes changed during our last test.
[05:33] Jasmine Cole: During failover you often see queueing pattern changes. Batching logic is adaptive - it looks at token latency targets and request interarrival time. If you suddenly shift traffic, initial batch sizes may be suboptimal. We recommend gating the failover in stages so that the serving runtime can stabilize batch windows. Also, consider pre-warming by sending synthetic traffic to initialize batching heuristics and KV caches.
[05:58] Marcus Reed: Any quantitative numbers on stabilization time?
[06:02] Ravi Kapoor: For our typical workloads, batch stabilizes in 1-3 minutes for short-seq dominated traffic; for long-context workloads it can be 5-10 minutes depending on token generation rates. KV cache warm-up to 80% effectiveness varies by session churn - anywhere from 10 minutes to an hour without cross-region replication.
[06:24] Henry Wong: If we do cross-region KV replication, what are the consistency semantics?
[06:29] Jasmine Cole: We treat KV cache as ephemeral performance cache - we prefer eventual consistency. We replicate prefixes asynchronously with TTL and frequency controls. For strict correctness you'd need application-level session state persisted to your DB, not KV cache.
[06:47] Karen Li: What about cost implications - egress and extra GPUs?
[06:51] Ravi Kapoor: Cross-region replication and extra warm standby capacity obviously add cost. We recommend capacity tiers: hot standby for critical customers (pre-warmed VMs/GPU with a commit) versus cold standby (spin up on failover with warm-up). Routing policies include cost weight so you can prefer cheaper region unless SLO breached.
[07:10] Ava Martinez: We also offer a burst policy where you allow short bursts to overflow to an alternative region for up to N minutes, which avoids spinning full fleets for rare spikes.
[07:20] Olga Petrova: Let's walk through a concrete DR playbook briefly.
[07:24] Ravi Kapoor: Step 0: Detect via telemetry + health checks. Step 1: Move non-critical traffic off impacted region using policy rule (gradual 25/50/75/100). Step 2: For sticky sessions, flag sessions for cache-populate ramp (10% sample). Step 3: Spin up or scale target region based on projected TPS; pre-warm KV with synthetic prompts for top N prefixes. Step 4: Monitor p95/p99 and hallucination metrics; if quality regresses, rollback to previous routing or route to an alternative model variant. Step 5: Post-incident audit and replication of missing cache keys if needed.
[08:05] Marcus Reed: In practice, how do you measure hallucination/regression in near real-time?
[08:11] Jasmine Cole: We rely on a small labeled set of canary prompts and automated heuristics (semantic divergence, token entropy). For customers with stricter needs, we can run a secondary correctness check in parallel and drop outputs that fail thresholds. There's latency cost though.
[08:32] Karen Li: Any gotchas for on-prem / Private deployments?
[08:37] Ravi Kapoor: Two big ones: networking topology and KMS. On-prem often has constrained egress and firewall rules - make sure the control plane endpoints and metrics ingest endpoints are routable if you want console visibility. KMS: some customers require hardware HSM only available on-prem. We support both but need to design cross-region key access carefully. Also, private deployments often prefer local model cache - that reduces cross-region pressure.
[09:04] Olga Petrova: Our compliance team will ask for runbooks and audit logs. Are those generated automatically?
[09:09] Ava Martinez: Yes, we emit audit logs for routing changes, playbook steps, and model version rollouts. We can send them to your SIEM or retain in our console with configurable retention.
[09:21] Henry Wong: Any edge cases we should worry about? For example, control plane partitioning causing split-brain routing?
[09:28] Ravi Kapoor: Good question. We avoid split-brain by requiring majority consensus in router controllers; if control plane loses reachability to a region, edge routers switch to local cached policy and fall back to conservative behavior (no global rollout). There's also a manual override for safety.
[09:45] Marcus Reed: Are there recommended SLOs for initiating failover? Like p95 > X ms for Y minutes?
[09:51] Jasmine Cole: Common thresholds: p95 > 2x baseline for 3 consecutive minutes or error rate spike > 5% over baseline for 2 mins. But it's customer-configurable. For Synapse's 250ms p95 target we might start graceful failover when p95 > 500ms sustained for 2 minutes.
[10:12] Ava Martinez: Quick note on observability - our console shows per-route token costs, latency heatmaps, and a failover simulator you can use to dry-run policies. We'll share access in the follow-up.
[10:25] Karen Li: OK, let's record next steps.
[10:28] Ava Martinez: Next steps recap: 1) We'll share the multi-region failover playbook (link below). 2) Schedule a 48-hour DR sim with Synapse team - Redwood to propose dates. 3) Exchange VPC/KMS network diagrams and decide on key replication approach. 4) We'll propose capacity profile for hot vs cold standby and estimated costs.
[10:45] Olga Petrova: We'll also send a small canary prompt set for regression checks.
[10:49] Ava Martinez: Great. Any last questions?
[10:52] Henry Wong: One small one - is there support for routing by customer tier dynamically?
[10:56] Ravi Kapoor: Yes - policies can include tenant-level weights/priority and tag matching. So you can prefer high-tier customers for hot standby.
[11:03] Karen Li: Thanks everyone, that was super helpful.
